newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin moves to sanatorium to step up workload.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin moves to sanatorium to step up workload.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, facing open heart surgery in the next two months, has moved from hospital to a sanatorium near Moscow and will be stepping up his workload there, the presidential press office said on Monday.
A brief Kremlin statement said Yeltsin's doctors had recommended the move to the Barvikha sanatorium. "The condition of the Russian president is quite satisfactory," it said.
A spokesman said Yeltsin, 65, would be able to increase his workload and be more physically active at Barvikha, a compound of government dachas and sanatoria located in woodland outside Moscow.
Yeltsin arrived at the sanatorium at the weekend and was already meeting officials there, starting with Igor Stroyev, the head of the Federation Council upper house of parliament, the spokesman said.

But the Kremlin said there were no plans to change the timeframe for Yeltsin's heart operation, which will graft in new veins to bypass blocked coronary arteries and improve the supply of blood to his heart.

Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and doctors say he may have had a third one in mid-summer before the second round of the Russian presidential election, in which he defeated a communist candidate by a handsome margin.

He had been in the exclusive Central Clinical Hospital since September 13 while doctors prepared him for the operation. A poorly-informed spokesman said earlier on Monday that Yeltsin was still in hospital.

The doctors complained previously that Yeltsin had ignored their advice on an energetic hunting trip after he was taken ill. Russian newspapers said the president shot a wild boar and dozens of ducks at the Rus hunting lodge.
"Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin), I'm not afraid to repeat it, is a difficult patient," Renat Akchurin, the Russian heart surgeon expected to lead the operation, said last month.
"There are difficult children as you know. As for Boris Nikolayevich, he is a difficult patient."
Yeltsin has looked stiff and spoken uneasily at several televised meetings with ministers, but doctors say bypass surgery could give the president a new lease on life.

Yeltsin spent three weeks in Barvikha during the summer and voted there in the second round of the presidential election on July 3, keeping the world's press waiting at the Moscow polling station where Kremlin leaders usually vote.
Aides said at the time that Yeltsin had a cold and was tired after a gruelling election campaign.
But the president, breaking a long Kremlin tradition of secrecy about the health of its leaders, said on September 5 that he would have a heart operation.

He has already delegated some powers to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who represented Russia at a weekend summit meeting of leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States to discuss the situation in Afghanistan.
Chernomyrdin is one possible presidential candidate if Yeltsin dies or has to step down before his term expires in 2000.
Another likely contender, national security adviser Alexander Lebed, was visiting the headquarters of the Western alliance NATO in Brussels on Monday.
